```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(patchwork)

penguins2 <- penguins |>
  select(species, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) |>
  drop_na()

overall_mod <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins2)
species_mod <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm + species, data = penguins2)
overall_r <- cor(penguins2$bill_length_mm, penguins2$bill_depth_mm)
overall_slope <- round(coef(overall_mod)[["bill_length_mm"]], 2)
species_slope <- round(coef(species_mod)[["bill_length_mm"]], 2)
by_species_r <- penguins2 |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(r = cor(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm), n = n())
```

## The Question

Bill length and bill depth are two of the simplest measurements a field biologist can take on a penguin, and both are used to distinguish species and track body condition in the Palmer Archipelago penguins studied by @gorman2014ecological. If you plotted every penguin's bill length against its bill depth without separating species, what would you conclude about how the two are related -- and would that conclusion still hold once you looked at each species on its own?

## What We Did

Using the `r nrow(penguins2)` penguins in the `palmerpenguins` dataset [@horst2020palmerpenguins] with complete bill measurements, we fit a simple linear regression of bill depth on bill length, first pooling all three species (Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo) together, and then again after adding species as a covariate. Comparing the two slopes -- and looking at the within-species correlations directly -- shows whether species is quietly driving the pooled result. All work was done in R [@rcore2026] with the tidyverse [@tidyverse2019] and ggplot2 [@ggplot22016].

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## What We Found

```{r}
#| label: fig-simpson-before-after
#| fig-cap: "Pooling across species (left) suggests bill depth decreases with bill length. Looking within each species (right) shows the opposite: bill depth increases with bill length in every species."
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
p_pooled <- ggplot(penguins2, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6, color = "#666666", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              color = "#25406A", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)",
       title = "All species pooled") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_species <- ggplot(penguins2, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0047B3", "#CC0033", "#00205B")) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)",
       title = "Same data, by species", color = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p_pooled | p_species
```

Pooling every penguin together (left) gives a negative correlation (Pearson's *r* = `r round(overall_r, 2)`, slope = `r overall_slope` mm of bill depth per mm of bill length): longer bills appear to go with shallower ones. But that pattern only exists because the three species differ both in typical bill length and in typical bill depth. Once species is added to the model (right), the slope flips sign entirely, to `r species_slope` -- and every species shows its own positive within-species correlation (@tbl-by-species-story). This reversal is a textbook example of **Simpson's paradox**: a grouping variable that is correlated with both the predictor and the outcome can invert the apparent relationship between them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-by-species-story
#| tbl-cap: "Within-species correlation between bill length and bill depth is positive for all three species."
#| echo: false
by_species_r |>
  mutate(r = round(r, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Species", "Correlation (r)", "n"))
```

## Why It Matters

Whenever a natural grouping variable is available -- species, site, cohort, or any other category that differs systematically in both predictor and outcome -- a pooled analysis should be treated as a starting point, not a conclusion. Checking whether a relationship holds up within each group is a cheap way to avoid reporting an effect that is really just an artifact of aggregation.

## What's Next

- Test whether the within-species slope itself differs by species (a length &times; species interaction).
- Add sex and island as further covariates.
